newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kuchma upbeat on foreign aid after Lazarenko quits.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma upbeat on foreign aid after Lazarenko quits.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma, speaking a day after accepting his reform-shy prime minister's resignation, said on Thursday he was sure Ukraine would get a delayed, multi-billion-dollar loan from the International Monetary Fund.

Kuchma, in south-west Ukraine to sign a deal on cooperation with the leaders of neighbouring Moldova and Romania, also said U.S. Vice President Al Gore had called him to say Washington still saw his country as a strategic partner.
Asked about the chance of winning a three-year, $2.5-$3 billion loan which has been cast in doubt by a six-month delay in passing the budget, Kuchma said: "I have no doubt in this".
The IMF has a mission in Kiev for talks until July 10 but it could not be immediately reached for comment.
The head of the Fund's Ukrainian office has said the IMF may issue a smaller, interim stand-by deal while Ukraine meets about 10 conditions left from a wish-list of 41.
Kuchma said Gore "confirmed the United States and Ukraine are strategic partners and that the U.S. administration would take this into account in its actions, including economic ones".

He added that a group of economic advisers would visit Ukraine on July 10 and 11 from the United States, whose desire to strengthen Ukrainian independence from Russia has put Kiev third in line after Israel and Egypt for U.S. cash.
Kuchma, who on Wednesday accepted the resignation of Pavlo Lazarenko said he would try to propose a new prime minister before parliament broke up for summer in mid-July.
Lazarenko's deputy Vasyl Durdynets is acting prime minister and Kuchma has decreed the cabinet should keep working.

The constitution gives him 60 days to re-appoint the government after a prime minister is sacked or resigns, but it is less clear on how long an acting premier can stay in place without parliamentary approval.
Lazarenko has been accused of failing to stamp out widespread corruption and to speed up reforms. He has denied allegations he raked in millions from the gas sector.
Kuchma said he met leaders of eight parliamentary groups on Wednesday to discuss the issue of the next prime minister, who will need the backing of 226 deputies in the 450-seat chamber.
"The new prime minister must take action because what kind of reforms are they if they only make things worse," he said.

No clear favourite has emerged from about a dozen possible candidates, and Kuchma faces a tough task finding someone reformist enough to keep foreign donors happy while satisfying the conservative-dominated parliament.

Analysts say Western officials and business people and Ukrainian reformers had been demanding Lazarenko's head for months. They pointed to Kuchma's apparent reluctance to sack him outright as a sign he feared his political and financial clout.
Lazarenko was removed from his post and taken to hospital on June 19 in what some analysts saw as a way for him to leave the premiership without losing face.
Few believe Lazarenko has left Ukraine's political stage forever, and he is seen as a potential candidate for presidential elections scheduled for October 1999.
